analysis.one_liner: Requires companies to test AI systems for discrimination and lets people appeal algorithmic decisions to a human.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by two Democratic senators, never received a hearing or vote and died in committee when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require companies that use algorithms to make high-stakes decisions about jobs, housing, credit, health care, insurance, and policing to test those systems for discrimination before and after use, publish summaries of those tests, and tell people when an algorithm was used. It would give people the right to a human decision and a human appeal instead of an algorithmic one, let them sue with $15,000-per-violation or triple damages, and let the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general enforce the rules. It died in the Senate Commerce Committee without any action.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who applies for a job, rent, a loan, insurance, or benefits, or who is screened by police, immigration, or election systems that use software to rank, score, or decide. The bill would let them demand a human alternative or appeal, see whether an algorithm was used, and sue if a system discriminates by race, sex, age, disability, income, or other protected traits. Workers reporting violations would gain whistleblower protection, and a new federal algorithm-auditing workforce would be created.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People judged by algorithms in hiring, housing, credit, and policing

how_it_helps.text: Bans offering or using a covered algorithm in a way that causes a disparate impact or otherwise discriminates on the basis of protected characteristics in decisions about employment, housing, credit, health care, utilities, insurance, criminal justice, elections, and government benefits [S2].

Requires a pre-deployment evaluation and an annual post-deployment impact assessment for any algorithm used in those consequential decisions, with an independent auditor when harm is plausible, and requires companies to publish summaries of the results [S2].

Directs the FTC to write rules giving people a no-cost way to opt out of an algorithmic decision and get a human alternative, plus a mechanism to appeal algorithmic decisions to a trained human reviewer [S2].

Creates a private right of action with treble damages or $15,000 per violation, invalidates pre-dispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers for claims under the Act, and authorizes FTC and state attorney general enforcement with civil penalties [S2].

Protects workers and others from retaliation for exercising their rights and from being fired for reporting violations, and directs federal agencies to build in-house algorithm-auditing capacity including up to 500 new FTC hires [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Companies that develop or deploy algorithms — from big tech platforms to banks, insurers, landlords, and employers using hiring or management software — would bear testing, auditing, disclosure, and compliance costs. Taxpayers would fund new FTC staff and auditors. Consumers could face some of the compliance cost passed through in prices, and small businesses with limited compliance capacity would face the same testing paperwork as large firms.
analysis.who_pays_short: Tech firms, employers, lenders, and insurers using algorithms

drawbacks.text: The definitions are broad: a 'covered algorithm' includes any computational process 'of similar or greater complexity' that affects a consequential action, and 'consequential action' sweeps in nearly every interaction with a business or government, so even small companies could face mandatory audits, disclosures, and litigation exposure for ordinary software [S2].

The private right of action allows treble damages or $15,000 per violation plus attorney fees for any violation of the transparency or testing rules, not just actual discrimination, which could drive a wave of lawsuits over paperwork errors and push companies to overcomply or pull products [S2].

The compliance machinery — independent audits, public disclosures in 10 languages, 5-to-10-year record retention, and a mandated public FTC repository of assessments — is costly, and some of it would likely be passed to consumers in prices; the bill also authorizes up to 500 new FTC personnel at taxpayer expense [S2].

Algorithmic auditing is an immature field with no settled standards, so early audit quality would vary, and the bill's own required disclosure warns that an audit 'does not guarantee that this algorithm is safe or in compliance with all applicable laws' [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core goal — stopping software from quietly discriminating in jobs, housing, credit, and policing — addresses real, documented harms, and the human-appeal and anti-retaliation provisions are the strongest parts. But the bill's breadth is a genuine weakness: it treats routine software as a regulated product, hands out large statutory damages for violations of testing and disclosure rules rather than only for actual discrimination, and would impose real compliance costs on small businesses as well as large ones. A narrower bill covering the highest-stakes decisions could have delivered much of the benefit at a fraction of the cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Markey introduced the Artificial Intelligence Civil Rights Act of 2024 on September 24, 2024, with Sen. Hirono as the sole cosponsor [S1][S3].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S4].
No further action appears in the record: the committee took up no hearing or markup, the Senate never voted, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing the bill [S4][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that develop or deploy algorithmic decision systems, and employers, lenders, insurers, and landlords that use them, are better off because the bill never advanced — they face no federal testing, auditing, disclosure, or private-litigation requirements for algorithmic discrimination.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Algorithm developers and the companies deploying them

sides.party_line_note: There was never a vote to measure party splits, but the bill's only support was two Democrats — the sponsor and one cosponsor — with no Republican backing, and it died in committee with no action.

industries.industry: AI and algorithm developers (software, platform, and data companies)
industries.note: The bill would make them test algorithms for discrimination before launch and each year after, publish assessment summaries, provide human alternatives and appeals, and face private lawsuits with $15,000-per-violation or treble damages. Those compliance and litigation costs exist today only under narrower, sector-specific rules, so the industry's interest in the bill's failure runs against people who are scored and sorted by these systems.

industries.industry: Employers, lenders, insurers, and landlords using hiring, credit, and screening software
industries.note: As deployers, they would share responsibility for discriminatory outcomes, would have to certify algorithms are safe before use, and could be sued by people their systems reject. Their interest in blocking the bill was aligned against applicants and tenants.

The bill would require independent audits by people with no financial stake in the systems they review, creating a large mandated market for audit services and a new federal occupational series and US Digital Service track for algorithm auditors. Because auditor independence is central to the bill's protections, the industry's growth runs alongside the public's interest.
